summary: Specifies a SOAP binding for BEEP, describing how SOAP messages are sent over BEEP. It was replaced by RFC 4227.

eli5.summary: SOAP messages need a way to travel. This says how to ship them using a different delivery service called BEEP. It has been replaced by RFC 4227.

subtitle: How to send SOAP messages using the BEEP protocol.

tldr.problem: SOAP is a messaging format for distributed applications, but it needs a reliable transport mechanism. BEEP is a general-purpose protocol for reliable exchanges, but had no SOAP binding.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies how SOAP 1.1 envelopes are transmitted and negotiated as a profile within BEEP, defining three message patterns (one-way, request-response, and request/N-responses), URL schemes, and port registration.
tldr.outcome: SOAP messages can now be sent reliably over TCP using BEEP as the transport. This specification was replaced by RFC 4227.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol) is an XML-based messaging protocol used to implement distributed messaging models including RPC, asynchronous event notification, and message forwarding. BEEP (Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol) is a framework for building reliable request-response protocols on top of TCP.

This RFC specifies the BEEP profile for SOAP, describing how SOAP 1.1 envelopes are transmitted using BEEP. The specification also provides a mechanism for negotiating new features of SOAP such as compression. The profile is identified by the URI http://iana.org/beep/soap.
sections.eli5: SOAP lets programs talk to each other using a standard message format. BEEP handles the reliable delivery. This RFC glues them together.

sections.title: BEEP Profile States and Initialization
sections.content:
The BEEP profile for SOAP has two states: boot and ready. When a channel is created, it starts in the boot state. The peer creating the channel sends a bootmsg element containing a mandatory resource attribute (similar to an HTTP path) and optional features attribute listing requested optional features.

If the server recognizes the resource, it replies with a bootrpy element, optionally listing which requested features it will support. The channel then enters the ready state. If the resource is not recognized or the message is malformed, the server sends an error reply and the channel remains in boot state.

The boot message serves two purposes: resource identification, allowing each channel to access a single network resource or service, and feature negotiation, allowing future SOAP enhancements like compression to be negotiated before message exchange begins.
sections.eli5: When SOAP over BEEP starts, the client says: I want to talk to resource X, and I can do these fancy tricks. The server says: OK, I know that resource, and I can do these tricks too. Then they start exchanging messages.

sections.title: Message Patterns and Transmission
sections.content:
SOAP over BEEP supports three message patterns. One-way messages involve the client sending a message without expecting a response; BEEP implements this as a one-to-many exchange where the server immediately sends a NUL (null) message. Request-response exchanges involve the client sending a message and the server returning a response; BEEP implements this with a MSG and RPY (reply) pair. Request/N-responses exchanges involve the client sending a message and receiving zero or more responses; BEEP implements this with a MSG followed by zero or more ANS (answer) messages and a final NUL.

SOAP envelopes are transmitted as UTF-8 text with the media type application/xml. Alternatively, a SOAP envelope can be transmitted as the root part of a multipart/related message with subordinate parts (such as images or documents) referenced using the rules of RFC 2387. SOAP faults are returned in regular RPY or ANS messages, never in BEEP ERR messages, even in request-response exchanges.
sections.eli5: There are three kinds of exchanges: fire-and-forget (send a message, no reply expected), ask-and-answer (send a question, get one answer), and ask-and-get-many (send a question, get zero or more answers). Each one maps to a BEEP message pattern.

sections.title: URL Schemes and Service Discovery
sections.content:
Two URL schemes are defined: soap.beep:// and soap.beeps://. The soap.beep scheme identifies SOAP resources transported over BEEP over TCP/IP. The soap.beeps scheme is identical except that the BEEP session must be tuned for privacy before the SOAP profile is started, either through a transport security profile or a user authentication profile supporting transport security.

Address resolution uses standard DNS mechanisms. If a URL contains a domain name and explicit port (e.g., soap.beep://server.example.com:1026), that port is used. If no port is specified, the SRV algorithm is used to query DNS for _soap-beep._tcp records; if none are found, a standard IANA-assigned port is used. If an IP address is present, DNS is not queried.
sections.eli5: SOAP over BEEP URLs look like soap.beep://server.example.com/resource. The computer looks up the server's address using DNS, and there is a secret version (soap.beeps) that encrypts the connection first.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
All implementations must support authentication via SASL DIGEST-MD5 and confidentiality via TLS with the TLS_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA cipher suite. Implementations may also offer MIME-based security services like OpenPGP or S/MIME. BEEP itself provides the detailed security mechanisms; this profile adds SOAP-specific considerations on top.

SOAP over BEEP can be vulnerable to denial-of-service attacks if an attacker sends pathological SOAP messages that are computationally expensive to parse or process. However, DV encoding (as referenced) does not exhibit significant non-uniformity in computational load. Receiver implementations should implement appropriate timeouts and resource limits.

RFC 3288 was obsoleted by RFC 4227 in 2005.
sections.eli5: Connections should be encrypted using standard security protocols. Servers should protect themselves from messages designed to waste computer time. The newer RFC 4227 replaced this one.
